newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French consumer spending falls in December.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French consumer spending falls in December.

text.p: French consumer spending fell in December, according to figures released on Thursday, the latest evidence that France's economy ended 1996 on a weak note.
But a finance ministry official told Reuters the overall financial and monetary outlook in Europe was positive and French growth should be fairly robust from the start of 1997.

National statistics institute INSEE said consumer spending on manufactured goods fell 0.8 percent in December after falling 0.5 percent in November, giving a drop of 3.4 percent over the last quarter of 1996.

"We were expecting a drop but a smaller drop than the one we saw. It confirms that consumer spending in the fourth quarter was pretty weak and that consumer spending's contribution to fourth-quarter gross domestic product will be negative," Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said.
"This shows that the recovery in the short term will be slow. We don't expect to see a robust rebound until the second half of 1997," David Naude, economist at JP Morgan, said.
The finance ministry official said December consumer spending may have been hit by the fact that winter sales did not start until January this year, rather than just after Christmas.
He also stressed that consumer spending had risen an average 3.1 percent over 1996, compared with 1.5 percent in 1995.
"There was a real acceleration in consumption," he said. Full-year consumption figures were compatible with forecasts made in the 1996 budget.

In 1997, the French economy would benefit from a favourable economic climate in Europe, and the boost to the economy from income tax cuts, he said. "The overall monetary and financial outlook in Europe is favourable," he said.
Low interest rates and a rise in the dollar are expected to help underpin economic growth this year.

The franc fell this week for the first time since 1994 below 5.50 per dollar, the level cited by ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing when he called in November for a franc devaluation to boost growth and jobs. Then the franc was trading at 5.08 per dollar.

The finance ministry official said there would also be a rise in household income early this year, due to a reduction in income tax and a decision to allow people to withdraw early 15 billion francs ($2.7 billion) from popular savings schemes (PEPs).
"Overall, from the start of the year, activity should be fairly robust," he said, adding there would be an acceleration through the year.

France needs solid growth this year to meet its target of reducing the budget deficit to three percent of GDP from four percent last year to qualify for European monetary union and help tackle unemployment, running at a record 12.7 percent.
The government is officially forecasting growth of 2.3 percent in 1997 after forecast 1.3 percent growth last year.
The weak consumption data followed news on Wednesday that manufacturing output fell in November for the third consecutive month.

Industrial production excluding energy, agri-food businesses and construction -- considered the best measure of manufacturing output -- fell 0.3 percent in November after a sharp 1.1 percent drop in October.
